title: SparkStream Staff Handbook
intro: How working at SparkStream actually operates: your standing on the team, duty and breaks, shifts and pay, the support and moderation queues, and what we hold about you. It describes practice rather than employment law. Where a section affects your pay or your contract, your contract is what governs.

content.text: Everyone here has the same standing. Ask anything, push back on anything, and say so when something looks wrong. That's how everything here gets decided, and it's the part of this handbook that matters most.
Nobody is expected to work something out alone. If you're stuck, unsure, or think a decision was wrong, saying so is the job. It isn't a complaint and it doesn't count against you.
If you disagree with something in this handbook, say that too. It gets rewritten when it's wrong.

There are four roles, each building on the one before it. Your role decides which tools the app shows you and which actions the server accepts from you. It does not change your standing: everything in the section above applies to every role equally.
Staff is the team's core role and where everyone starts: the support queue, reviewing reports and held content, and user lookups. Most of the day-to-day work in this handbook is Staff work.

Staff Lead adds the decisions that affect a person rather than a queue item: formal warnings, community bans, removing someone's messaging access, the more serious moderation reviews, and tickets other staff have passed up. Leads also handle credit rewards and giveaway codes.

Admin adds running the team itself: inviting and certifying staff, posting shifts, contracts, payroll and time off, refunds, platform-level account decisions, and granting the Staff roles. Admins also hold the audit and security logs.
Admin Lead adds the small set of controls that affect everyone at once, such as marketing sends and site-wide promotions, and managing Admins. Admin Leads are appointed by the company owner directly.

Above all four sits the owner, who runs the company. The owner role is not grantable in the app at all: it is fixed in the server's configuration, which is also why nobody, at any rank, can change or remove it from inside the app. The owner appoints and removes Admin Leads, holds the development and testing tools, sets the pay ladder, is not paid hourly, and never appears in payroll. The owner is exempt from shift posting and certification, because those mechanisms exist to protect and pay scheduled staff and the owner is neither. Every standard in this handbook about conduct, fairness and privacy applies to the owner exactly as it applies to anyone else.

items: A role change is always made by someone above the role in question, with a recorded reason, and you are told when it happens
Passing something to a role above yours is correct handling, never a failure
No role changes the standard you work to, or your standing on the team

content.text: Pay is set by role, in the system, and nowhere else. Everyone in a role is paid exactly the same rate, and a change to a rate applies to the whole role at once. That is deliberate: it makes equal pay for the same work a property of the system rather than a promise, because there is nowhere a different number could be entered for one person.

items: Staff: 14 GBP per hour
Staff Lead: 16 GBP per hour
Admin: 18 GBP per hour
Admin Lead: 20 GBP per hour

content.text: These are the current rates; when the ladder changes, this handbook is updated with it, and the app always shows your live rate in My Employment. The rates always sit above the UK National Living Wage. A change of role and the pay that goes with it take effect together, never separately.

SparkStream handles people's accounts, their money, and things they've said in private. The standard is that a person on the other end of anything you do would think it was handled fairly if they could see exactly what you did.

items: Decide on what's in front of you, not on who it involves
If you can't justify an action in a sentence, don't take it yet
When two readings are both defensible, take the one that's easier to undo

content.text: Getting something wrong after thinking it through is fine and expected. Guessing quietly because you didn't want to ask is the thing to avoid.
On Duty tells the queue you're actively working. It's what routes new work to you, and it's what counts your paid hours.
You can only clock on once a shift has been posted for you, and once an admin has certified you. Every app launch starts you Away on purpose, so clock on again at the start of each session.

If the app closes while you're on duty, through a crash, an update, or the tray, the shift is not left running: the next time you open the app it clocks you off, and the server closes it at your posted end regardless. Nothing is ever paid past the shift that was posted.
Reading a queue works whether you're on duty or not. Acting on real items needs you clocked on.
Going on duty gives you paid break tokens sized to your posted shift.

items: Under 4 hours: one break
4 to 6 hours: two breaks
Over 6 hours: three breaks

content.text: Taking a break starts a 20 minute paid countdown. You keep getting paid and stop receiving new work until you come back, or until the timer runs out, which moves you to unpaid Away automatically so a forgotten break can't quietly bill time you weren't working. There's a 45 minute cooldown between breaks.
Off Duty is always available regardless of break state. Use it any time you're genuinely stepping away.

Shifts an admin posts for you appear in My Employment under Upcoming shifts, and you'll be told when one is assigned. Clocking on inside a shift sizes your break tokens for it. A posted shift appears up to an hour ahead as a countdown, but you cannot clock on before it starts, because paid time starts at the posted start either way. A 15 minute wrap-up window after the posted end still counts.

Admins can also post open shifts with no assignee, and the first to take one gets it. Taking a shift is always your choice; you're never put on one automatically. It's refused only if it clashes with a shift you already hold, falls inside a recorded absence, would breach your 40 hour cap, was offered as non-overtime and would put you over your contracted hours, or you have a working time change pending.
If you can't work a shift, you can offer it for cover or ask an admin to release you. It stays yours until somebody takes it or an admin decides, so nothing is ever left unattended because you asked.

Your contract sets a number of hours per week. Admins can only schedule you up to that number. Anything beyond it counts as overtime and has to be deliberately confirmed when the shift is offered, so it's never a surprise.
Overtime just means a shift would put you over your contracted hours for that week. The exact numbers are shown up front when you take one.
Overtime isn't paid at a higher rate, because the base rate is already set well above what this work usually pays. It's offered as a choice and never as an expectation.

Separately from your contracted hours, there is a hard weekly cap: no more than 40 hours of shifts in any week. That is our own limit, set deliberately below the legal 48-hour average, and by default nothing can be scheduled past it, whether by an admin or by you taking open shifts.

If you want to be able to work past 40 hours, you can opt out in My Employment. It is a checkbox only you can tick: it is entirely voluntary, nobody will ever ask you to tick it, and declining has no consequences of any kind.

A change in either direction takes effect 7 days after you request it, and while it is pending you cannot take on new shifts. That notice period is what makes the choice deliberate for both sides: nobody can stack hours ahead of a cap they know is coming back, and nobody can be rushed into lifting one.

Shifts you have already accepted always stand. Restoring the cap stops anything new being scheduled past 40 hours; it never cancels work you agreed to. My Employment shows you any upcoming weeks already over the cap, and offering cover from the Shifts panel in My Employment is the way to reduce them if you want to.
Pro subscribers, staff, and holders of the Myth Made Real achievement are automatically high priority and appear at the top of the Open queue. Everyone else sits below at normal priority.
Never deprioritise on anything the app hasn't already sorted for you. Every ticket gets answered.

You can reply and keep a ticket open, or reply and close it. If a user replies again after a close, it reopens automatically and returns to the Open queue with the full conversation attached, so it's never a fresh unrelated issue to them.
Keep replies clear and free of jargon unless the person has shown they want the technical detail. Say what you did, what happens next, and what they should do if it doesn't work.
Closed tickets leave the queue 48 hours after the last staff reply. The user's own device keeps their copy regardless, so they can still reopen it later.

Some actions belong to roles above yours. If a ticket needs something you can't do, escalate it rather than improvising. Escalated tickets leave your queue and are picked up by Admins. Refunds, permanent access grants, and adding or removing staff roles are Admin work too; any staff member can issue or revoke a time-limited Pro grant.
Escalate early rather than late. An escalation isn't a failure to handle something; it's the correct handling.
Add a note saying what you've already established. The person picking it up should not have to redo your reading.

sections.title: What you see, and what you do with it

content.text: Working here gives you sight of things people did not choose to share with you personally: their tickets, their reports, their account history.

items: Never share what you see outside the team
Never use it for anything other than resolving the thing in front of you
Never look something up out of curiosity

content.text: Some records are access logged, and you'll be told at the point of access when that's the case. That isn't suspicion of you; it's what lets us tell a person honestly who has seen their information.

Direct messages between users are end to end encrypted: nobody at SparkStream can read a conversation. Reporting is the one exception, and a narrow one. When someone reports a message, the app sends that message plus the five before it for context, and that bundle is readable by the moderation team. Nothing else in the conversation is, and there is no way to ask for more.
Staff accounts can reach other people's data and the business itself, so they carry an extra layer ordinary accounts don't: SparkStream recognises the networks you work from.

items: Sign in from a network we haven't seen you on before and staff access pauses until you enter a 6-digit code emailed to your account address. Codes are freshly random each time, last 30 minutes, and five wrong attempts kill the code, tell you by email and in the app, and raise a security alert.

The same email carries a red button for when it wasn't you. It signs out every session on your account and locks your staff access; an admin restores it once your account is secured. Change your Twitch password straight away as well.

Someone above you can also lock your staff account outright while something is looked into, and only someone above you can lift it. A lock is not a sanction and not a demotion: your role and your employment record are untouched by it.

A lock is paid. You are not working because we stopped you working, so you are paid in full for the whole of it, on exactly the same basis as a suspension: whichever is greater of your average weekly hours over your last eight normal weeks or your contracted week, fixed at the moment the lock goes on. Your paid leave keeps building at the same rate, and any shifts in your diary are put up for cover so you are not marked down for missing them. That holds however the lock started, including when you set it off yourself by reporting a sign-in you did not recognise: telling us your account may be compromised is the right thing to do, and it will never cost you money.

content.text: What this stores: never your actual IP address. We keep a scrambled per-person code derived from the network, which can't be reversed and can't be matched across people, plus a masked form like 86.152.x.x used in the email and admin alerts. Your first network is trusted automatically. Keep an email address on your account: without one, every new network needs an admin to approve it. The owner account is warned rather than blocked, because a broken email path would otherwise lock out the one account able to fix it.
None of this applies to ordinary use of SparkStream as a user. It guards the staff surface only.

sections.title: Confirming who you are talking to

content.text: Anyone can type a username into a ticket. Before you act on anything sensitive or destructive, a refund, a deletion, an unlock, an account change, confirm you are talking to the account holder.

items: Never ask for the number itself. Use Request verification, in the ticket or in User Management, and the person confirms in their own app: their PIN, or their card's last 4 digits if they haven't set one. You only ever see the result.

Where they have neither, a codeword is emailed to them to put in their stream title, and you confirm only whether it appeared. That is the last rung. Below it there is nothing but admin judgement, and we do not ask anyone for ID.

You cannot verify yourself, and you can only ask someone below your own rank. Ordinary users are below everyone, so normal support work is unaffected. Each person can only be asked once a minute, because every request emails them.

The server holds you to it: unlocking an account or resetting a PIN refuses until a fresh verification exists. If the person has nothing to verify with, it proceeds and is logged as having done so unverified.
A red disavowal means exactly what it says: whoever is in your conversation is not the account holder. Do not act on that conversation, and tell an admin.

content.text: Verification requests also email the account holder, so the real person knows even when someone else is holding their session. Your request is logged against your name, and the verification itself is recorded on their account with the method and the time.
Moderation decisions are about content and behaviour, never about the person. Two people doing the same thing get the same outcome.

items: Act on what was actually posted or done, not on what you suspect was meant
Prefer the reversible action while you're still unsure
Record a reason that would make sense to the person it's about

content.text: Every outcome has to answer two questions: what happens to the content, and what happens to the person. If your action only answers one of them, it isn't finished.
Reporters are told their report was reviewed and whether we acted, never what was done or to whom. Your written reason goes to the person the action is about, so write it for them.
If a case involves you, someone you know, or anything you have a stake in, hand it to someone else. That's not a rule about trust, it's about the decision being defensible afterwards.

An admin can place practice items in the real queues for you. They're fabricated from top to bottom, no real person is involved, and they behave like real items so the tools become familiar before they matter. They are always clearly marked as tests, you can work them while you're off the clock, and they skip the identity check a real ticket needs.
Practice works even before you're certified, which is the point: you should not be learning the tools on somebody's actual problem.

Afterwards you can see what was expected and why. Only the clearest held post, forum report and DM report cases are marked automatically. Everything harder than that, and every other kind of practice case, goes to an admin to mark beside the model answer, because a training tool that marks a reasonable call wrong teaches you to distrust it.

Nothing from practice is written into your employment record and it is never grounds for discipline. What an admin can see is a summary of how your recent practice went, worked out fresh each time the page loads and stored nowhere, so somebody can offer you a hand rather than let you struggle quietly. You see the same summary about yourself.
Before your first shift an admin certifies you. Until that happens you can't clock on at all, which also means you can't start being paid.
Three things have to be true first, and the system refuses to certify you without them:

items: Your contract is on file, including your contracted hours. Your pay rate comes from your role (see Roles on the team). If you're employed through an employer of record, that provider is named instead

Your employment information is on file: your legal name, date of birth, address and phone number, and an emergency contact name and number. If you're employed through an employer of record, only your name, phone number and emergency contact are needed here, because that provider holds the rest
You've read this handbook and confirmed it

content.text: The first of those is the company's job, not yours. Nobody can be put to work here before the terms they're working under actually exist, and that isn't something an admin can wave through in a hurry.
Everything else on your Getting started checklist is useful rather than mandatory.

Certification can be withdrawn from Staff and Staff Leads, for example while retraining. If that happens you're told, and you're told why. Admin accounts cannot be de-certified; a lock is the tool there.
We'd rather tell you this plainly than have you discover it.

items: Hours worked, tickets answered and response times are recorded
Fabricated practice cases are placed in the real queues. They are always clearly marked as tests, never covert, and nothing you do on one counts towards your figures
Access to the most sensitive records is logged

content.text: None of this is scored against you individually as a target. Time a ticket sits overdue before anyone has claimed it is shared across whoever was on duty rather than pinned on one person, because an unclaimed backlog is a staffing problem. Once a ticket is yours, time past the target counts with you, which is the part you can actually do something about.
If something in these figures looks unfair, say so. It's been changed before on exactly that basis.

My Employment holds your contract, contracted hours, rate, hours actually worked this week and month, and an estimated pay figure where a rate is on file. That figure is estimated from hours worked, is before tax and deductions, and is a convenience total rather than a payslip.

Your legal name, date of birth, address, phone number, National Insurance or tax number, and emergency contact are held encrypted. If you're employed through an employer of record, we hold less, because they hold your payroll identity.
An admin reading those details leaves an audit entry, and the button says so before they press it.
Your record also holds anything written down about your work: notes, a promotion or a change of pay, times we offered support, and, if it ever comes to it, a concern raised or a formal warning.

You can read all of it, any time, on My Record. There is no second version of your file kept somewhere you cannot see. Anything you are asked to acknowledge stays marked as waiting until you confirm you have read it, and you are the only person who can confirm it.
An entry written in error is withdrawn rather than deleted, with the reason attached, so you can see both that it was there and why it no longer stands.
We never ask for your bank details in the app. Payment details are collected in the payroll process outside it.
If something in your record is wrong, say so. You are entitled to a copy of everything we hold about you, and to have what is inaccurate corrected.

sections.title: If you are suspended from duties

content.text: Sometimes something has to be looked into, and the fair way to do that is with you out of the middle of it. Being suspended from duties means you are asked not to work while that happens. It is not a punishment, it is not a finding, and it is not a dismissal. It says nothing about the outcome, because there isn't one yet.

You are paid in full for the whole of it. Full means a real number, not a reassurance: your pay is set at whichever is greater, your average weekly hours over your last eight normal weeks or your contracted week, and it is fixed at the moment the suspension starts. It cannot drift down while it runs, however long it runs. You are told the figure when it begins, it is on your own pay screen throughout, and it goes to payroll as a paid period the same way sick leave does.

Everything else about your employment carries on unchanged. Your role, your rate and your contract are untouched. Your paid leave keeps building up at the same rhythm, exactly as it does through sickness. Any shifts already in your diary are put up for cover, so you are not marked down for missing work you were told not to do.

You are told why, in writing, in words you can read for yourself, and with a date it will be looked at again. It is kept as short as we can manage. If it has to run past that date, you are told that it is continuing and given a fresh reason, because a suspension nobody has to justify twice is how somebody ends up sitting at home for a month.

items: You keep your own record, your own pay and hours, and your own shift history, and you can read all of it while suspended
You keep the right to answer, and to appeal anything that ends up written down
You are not suspended for raising a concern. That is covered separately, and doing it is protected

content.text: A suspension is not the same as a security lock on your account. A lock is about whether your sign-in can be trusted right now, usually after an unrecognised sign-in, and it says nothing at all about your work. The app tells you which one you are looking at. They are paid the same way, for the same reason: in both cases it is us stopping you working.
You get paid annual leave. UK law sets the standard we work to, and if your own country entitles you to more than that, you get the better of the two.

Three base days are added on top of what you build up, each leave year. In your first weeks they unlock in steps rather than all at once: the first day once you have been certified two weeks and worked 16 hours since, the second at four weeks and 40 hours, the third at eight weeks and 80 hours. Both clocks run from certification, because that is when you can first be put to work. The steps keep flexibility arriving early while making sure paid leave always tracks real work, and My Employment, under Time off and leave, shows you exactly where you are against the next one.
The steps are climbed once, ever: once you have passed the last of them, every later leave year's three days are available from its first day.

On top of those, leave builds up as you work, at the statutory rate of 12.07% of the hours you work. In round terms that's about an hour of paid leave for every eight hours worked. There's no cap: a heavier month earns more leave, always.
It's counted in hours rather than days because shifts here vary in length. Counting in days would mean guessing how long your day is, and that guess would be wrong for somebody.
The leave year runs 1 April to 31 March.

Booking leave costs you the hours you were scheduled to work in that period. If no shifts were posted across the dates you book, it costs you nothing, because there was nothing to take off. Your balance and what each booking used are both shown in My Employment, under Time off and leave.

sections.title: What happens to leave you don't take

content.text: At the end of the leave year, whatever you haven't taken goes one of three ways.

items: The part you built up from hours worked this year carries over into the next leave year, once
Anything still left of what you carried in from the year before lapses: leave rolls over one year and no further
Whichever of the three base days you have unlocked, and anything extra added on top, are paid to you instead. Days that never unlocked are not paid out, because they were never yours to take

content.text: Leave you take is counted against the oldest part of your balance first: carried hours before this year's, this year's before the paid-out pot. That's deliberate and in your favour, because the part closest to lapsing is always the part being spent.

The one-year limit exists because statutory leave is for resting, not for banking: without it, years of untaken leave could pile into months of paid absence, which helps nobody and least of all the person who never rested. The law works the same way, and is in fact stricter than this.

You will never lose leave silently. The app reminds you to take your leave as the year end approaches, more insistently the closer it gets, and tells you exactly what would lapse and when. If leave is about to lapse, an admin is told too, so getting you time off becomes the team's job rather than something you were supposed to remember alone. Leave you couldn't take because of sickness or family leave doesn't lapse: tell an admin and those hours are added back to your balance, with the reason attached so you can see exactly what changed and why.

The balance shown in the app is a record of your entitlement, not a payslip. Actual payment goes through payroll. If the two ever disagree, payroll is the one that counts and the app is the one that's wrong.

Report sick from My Employment in the Staff Hub, under Sickness and absence. There is no approval step, because being ill is a notification, not a request. The moment you report it, your upcoming shifts are offered to the team for cover, admins are told, and you are done: rest.

Sick pay runs from day one. There are no unpaid waiting days here, whatever the law of the day allows. For the first six weeks of a sickness you are paid your full average earnings, worked out over your last eight normal weeks, the same as the first weeks of family leave. After that, the statutory rate applies for as long as the law provides. Payment itself goes through payroll.
You can self-certify for up to seven days. Past seven days we ask for a fit note from a doctor, which is the standard rule and the only paperwork involved.

items: Your paid leave keeps building up while you are off sick, at your normal rhythm

If you fall ill during booked annual leave, tell an admin: those days count as sick leave and the holiday hours are added back to your balance. The booking itself stays on your record and the correction sits beside it, so you can see both rather than one quietly replacing the other
Nothing can be scheduled for you while a sickness is recorded, and you cannot pick up shifts either. Rest is the job

content.text: When you are better, end the sickness from the same place you reported it. Nobody chases you while it is open.

Maternity leave is up to 52 weeks, with 39 of them paid: the first six weeks at your full average earnings, worked out over your last eight normal weeks, then the statutory rate for the rest. The law asks for 90% in those first weeks; we pay all of it, because the difference is small to the company and not small to you.
Paternity leave is two weeks at the same first-weeks terms, takeable together or separately within the first year.

An admin records the leave with you, and from then on nothing can be scheduled into it. Your paid annual leave keeps building up for the whole duration at your normal rhythm, which is your legal right and the system's default rather than something to ask for.
Payment goes through payroll, like all money. Where your own country's law gives you more than any of this, you get the more, as everywhere else in this handbook.

sections.title: Changing your details and requesting time off

content.text: You can update where you're based and the hours you usually work yourself, once every 30 days. Inside that window the change becomes a request an admin approves, because availability changing at will fights the shift scheduler. Either way you hear back.
Time off is requested in whole days from My Employment in the Staff Hub, under Time off and leave. You're told when it's decided, and the reason if it's declined.
Your country and working window are recommendations to whoever is planning cover. They never restrict what you can be offered or what you can take.

If you're employed through an employer of record, your leave is worked out here on exactly the same terms as everyone else's, and your employer of record administers it. The terms in this handbook are a floor, never a ceiling: where your own country's law grants you more, you get the more. Requests still go through My Employment, under Time off and leave, so cover can be planned.
Staff earn referral credits like anyone else. Your code still works and credits still build up while you're on staff.
You're never expected or asked to market SparkStream. It's entirely optional.
Credits you build up sit untouched while you're staff, and only start counting down as Pro days after your staff access ends. Referring is a genuine perk with no downside, not part of the job.
If you make a mistake, say so as early as you can. Almost everything here is reversible if it's caught quickly, and the cost of a late disclosure is always higher than the mistake.

If you're concerned about something somebody else did, including an admin or the owner, raise it. For anyone below the owner, there is always a route that does not go through the person you're worried about.

Honesty about a limit: SparkStream is currently a very small company with no separate HR function, so a concern about the owner will, at this size, be read by the owner. We would rather say that plainly than pretend a route exists that does not. What is promised instead: every concern raised gets a written answer, raising one is never held against you, and your employment record is fully visible to you, so any consequence would have to happen somewhere you can see it.

There are also routes that do not involve the owner at all. If you are employed through an employer of record, their HR and grievance process is independent of SparkStream. Anyone in the UK can contact Acas free of charge and in confidence, and a protected disclosure to a regulator is protected by law whatever the size of the employer. We will not pretend a future HR function would change this: in an owner-run company, HR is hired by the owner and cannot hold real power over the owner. The genuinely independent routes are the external ones, which is exactly why they are named here.
If you think a rule in this handbook is wrong, or that following it would produce an unfair outcome, say so before following it.
